_about: How passages have been read at different times. A reading is listed, not endorsed; the Church's own teaching is in the Teaching tab.

stages.label: Greek Old Testament
stages.note: The Greek text has a masculine pronoun ('he shall bruise'), referring to the 'seed', which later readers took as a single descendant.

stages.label: Irenaeus (2nd century)
stages.note: Read Mary as the new Eve in the line of this promise, though not directly in this verse.

stages.label: Latin Vulgate
stages.note: Many Latin manuscripts read 'she' (ipsa); the Clementine edition does. The Hebrew has a masculine pronoun, and the debate is old.

stages.label: Modern Catholic reading
stages.note: The Catechism speaks of a 'proto-evangelium' without requiring that Mary is the subject of this verse (CCC 410-411).

stages.label: In its own time
stages.note: A child in the days of King Ahaz, as a sign that the house of David would not fall.

stages.label: The Greek Old Testament
stages.note: The translators rendered the Hebrew 'almah' (young woman) as parthenos (virgin).

stages.label: Matthew
stages.note: Reads the child as fulfilled in the conception of Jesus (Matthew 1:22-23).

stages.label: Fathers
stages.note: Justin Martyr, Irenaeus and others defended the Christian reading against the Jewish reading.

stages.label: The Fathers
stages.note: Read the rock as Peter, as Peter's confession, or as Christ himself; many Fathers allowed more than one.

stages.label: Rome
stages.note: The bishop of Rome claimed the commission of Peter from the early centuries.

stages.label: The Reformation
stages.note: Protestant interpreters tended to say the rock was Peter's confession or Christ.

stages.label: Vatican I and II
stages.note: Teach that Christ made Peter the visible head of the Church (CCC 881).

stages.label: The early Church
stages.note: Ignatius of Antioch called the Eucharist 'the medicine of immortality' around AD 110.

stages.label: Augustine
stages.note: Read the passage with a strong sense of the sacrament and the spiritual reality.

stages.label: The Reformation
stages.note: Some reformers took the chapter as spiritual only; Luther held the Real Presence; Zwingli a memorial.

stages.label: Trent
stages.note: Teaches that the Eucharist contains the body and blood of Christ truly, really and substantially.

stages.label: Origen and the Greek Fathers
stages.note: Stressed human freedom and God's foreknowledge.

stages.label: Augustine
stages.note: Developed a strong doctrine of grace and predestination against Pelagius.

stages.label: The Reformation
stages.note: Calvin took the chapter in the direction of double predestination.

stages.label: Council of Trent and later
stages.note: Teaches that God's grace precedes our will and that we can resist it; the Church condemns the teaching that anyone is predestined to evil.

stages.label: Philo and Origen
stages.note: Read the days as figures for an ordered creation, not as twenty-four-hour days.

stages.label: Basil of Caesarea
stages.note: In his Hexaemeron he took the days with a literal sense but a theological interest.

stages.label: Augustine
stages.note: In The Literal Meaning of Genesis he argued that God created all things at once, with the days as an order of knowledge, and warned against embarrassing the faith by foolish claims about nature.

stages.label: The 20th century
stages.note: Pius XII and Vatican II (Dei Verbum 12) allowed that genre and the ancient setting matter.

stages.label: Rabbi Akiva
stages.note: Held that the Song is the holy of holies of Scripture, about God and Israel.

stages.label: Origen
stages.note: Read it as Christ and the soul or the Church, in a commentary that shaped the Latin tradition.

stages.label: Bernard of Clairvaux
stages.note: Preached eighty-six sermons on the first chapters, on the soul and Christ.

stages.label: Modern interpreters
stages.note: Recover the literal reading as human love, while the Church's tradition keeps the spiritual sense.

stages.label: Papias and Irenaeus
stages.note: Read the thousand years as a literal reign on earth before the end.

stages.label: Augustine
stages.note: Read it as the time of the Church between the first and second coming, and not as a future earthly kingdom.

stages.label: The Church today
stages.note: The Catechism rejects forms of millenarianism that foresee a worldly triumph before the end (CCC 676).

stages.label: Clement of Alexandria
stages.note: Wrote 'Who Is the Rich Man That Shall Be Saved?', reading the call to give as a call to inner detachment.

stages.label: Francis of Assisi
stages.note: Took the passage as a personal call to literal poverty.

stages.label: The tradition
stages.note: Distinguishes the commandments, for everyone, from the counsels of perfection, for those called (CCC 915).

stages.label: Origen and Augustine
stages.note: Read the story allegorically: the traveller is Adam, the Samaritan Christ, the inn the Church.

stages.label: Modern interpreters
stages.note: Tend to read it as a parable with one main point about neighbour love, while the allegorical reading continues in the tradition.

entries.title: The cry of the righteous sufferer

stages.label: In Israel
stages.note: A psalm of lament that ends in praise.

stages.label: The Gospels
stages.note: Draw on it in the passion accounts: the dividing of the garments, the mocking, the cry of abandonment.

stages.label: The Fathers
stages.note: Read it as the voice of Christ, praying through the psalms.

stages.label: Jewish tradition
stages.note: Many Jewish readers have seen the Servant as Israel; some medieval commentators held that view against Christian readings.

stages.label: Acts 8
stages.note: Philip explains the passage to the Ethiopian as good news about Jesus.

stages.label: The Fathers
stages.note: Read it as a prophecy of the passion of Christ.

stages.label: In Paul's time
stages.note: A baptismal statement about unity in Christ across ethnic, social and sexual lines.

stages.label: Across history
stages.note: Has been cited in debates about slavery and about the roles of women.

stages.label: The Church today
stages.note: Reads it with the understanding that equal dignity does not erase difference (CCC 369-372).

stages.label: Augustine
stages.note: Said that James is correcting those who misread Paul.

stages.label: Luther
stages.note: Called it an 'epistle of straw', in comparison to John and Paul.

stages.label: Trent
stages.note: Teaches that justification is by grace through faith and that faith is made alive by charity.

stages.label: The early Church
stages.note: Used the passage in debates on whether those who had apostatised could be readmitted.

stages.label: Novatian
stages.note: Argued that grave sin after baptism could not be forgiven by the Church.

stages.label: The Church
stages.note: Rejected the Novatian position and taught that there is a way back through penance.
